⚡ Can the AI and energy revolutions grow without deepening water stress?
 
As World Water Week 2026 continues in Stockholm under the theme "Water for People and Progress," this is the question I keep coming back to: AI is no longer only an energy story.
 
By 2027, AI is projected to withdraw 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water annually, up to six times Denmark's total annual water withdrawal. Cooling is a major part of the equation. Data centres generate enormous amounts of heat, and removing that heat can require significant volumes of water, especially in hot climates.
 
I have come to see this as a siting and governance question rather than a technology one. Where digital infrastructure is built, and under what rules, will determine whether it strengthens or strains local water systems.
Three approaches are worth watching:
 
📐 Set measurable standards. Singapore's Green Data Center Roadmap prioritises energy efficiency and cooling technologies suited to tropical climates, and steers new development toward areas with cleaner grids and more abundant resources.
 
💧 Make water conditions part of approval. Malaysia, South-East Asia's most water-stressed country, has more than 100 proposed data centres that could consume over 808 million litres a day. Regulators now require all new facilities to use only recycled, reclaimed or rainwater as a condition of approval.
 
🌍 Plan for local conditions, not imported models. In Asia and the Pacific, water-use effectiveness averages 1.65 litres per kilowatt-hour, more than three times the global average of 0.5. Cooling strategies that work in Stockholm will not work in Kuala Lumpur.
 
For countries across the Global South, the opportunity is not simply to host the next generation of digital infrastructure, but to shape how it is powered, cooled and governed.
 
The AI revolution will be judged not only by what it computes, but by what it consumes.
